Causes of deaths

Report generated on Date: 2022-12-16 Time: 14:38

1 Aim

We aim at exploring the different mortality causes by age in 2020 in Switzerland.

2 Data

2.1 Causes of deaths

We received the number of deaths by week from 1995 to 2020, by age group and sex, overall and stratified by cause. 32 different causes are mentioned:

Note that some causes are included in other causes. For instance suicide (“31. Suizid”) is included in the number of total accident (“30. Unfälle insgesamt”).

In addition we also analyse the remaining deaths (i.e. deaths not from the seven selected causes), which is obtained by removing the deaths from the main causes to the total number of deaths (called “tot.other”).

2.2 Reported deaths

2.2.1 By cause and age, over calendar year

2.2.2 Comparison with mortality reported by FSO

We compare the total number of deaths by age group and by year (internally) reported in this dataset to the total number of deaths reported on the FSO website.

We observe some discrepancy. The number of deaths by cause is consistently higher for people aged <80 an lower for 80+ over the year. When looking at the total number of deaths, we observe little difference between the two datasets.

In 2020, the estimated total number of deaths was lower in the dataset reporting the cause of deaths by a bit more than 1,000 people.

2.2.3 Comparison with data from excess mortality

We then compare these two mortality datasets to a third one: the mortality reported through the estimates of excess mortality by FSO (available here). As this latter dataset only reports mortality by two age groups (0-64, >65), we can only compare the total number of deaths estimated in these three datasets over time.

The number of deaths reported in the excess mortality dataset (green) seems to be very slightly but consistently lower than the mortality reported by the FSO (red). The mortality by cause of deaths is also slightly different from these two datasets, showing less variability over the years.

2.3 Population

To predict the mortality risk by age group, we need to adjust for the population size. We retrieve the population for each age group on the 1st of January of each year from FSO website and interpolate it to obtain the weekly population.

3 Analysis

3.1 Fitting mortality 2010-2019

For each cause and each age group, we use the weekly mortality data in 2010-2019 to predict the weekly mortality in 2020. We assumed that the number of deaths \(y_{i}(t)\) due to a given cause in given age group at time \(t\) for sex \(i\) followed a Poisson distribution: \[y_{i}(t)\sim Poisson(\mu_{i}(t))\]

We model the changes of mortality risk over time using two Gaussian Processes (GPs). We use an offset for the total population \(N\) in the given age group:

\[\log\mu_{ijk} = \alpha + \beta_{F}\mathbb{1}_{i=F} + f(t) + g(t) + \log(N)\] where \(\alpha\) is the intercept,\(\beta_F\) is the effect of being a female on the mortality and \(N\) is the population. The GP \(f\) models the long-term trend in mortality over time while the GP \(g\) represents the change in mortality over the weeks of the year. We assume an exponential quadratic Kernel for \(f\) and a periodic Kernel for \(g\).

3.2 Excess mortality

The model provides estimates of the weekly expected mortality by cause and age class in 2020. We obtain the excess mortality by subtracting the expected mortality to the reported number of deaths.
